629	
630	_The questions are Claude Code's proposals of 2026-10-22; the author divided the first into two
631	(15.1 and 15.2) when answering. In 15.1–15.4, the parts marked as drafted give facts, computed with
632	Claude Code (Opus 5.5) by script from batch-1's records (14) and from section 11, which is
633	unchanged. The answers, marked "Answer (author)", are the author's, copied from the conversation of
634	2026-10-22. After Claude Code's review, the author added the last two sentences of 15.4, which say
635	why the predictions were off, and at the author's request Claude Code applied the review's wording
636	"median wall time" in 15.1 and "median peak total RSS" in 15.3._
637	
638	### 15.1 (a) Wall time
639	
640	> How do the two implementations compare end to end in wall time?
641	
642	_Drafted with Claude Code (Opus 5.5): the medians are in 14.6, and d1, d2 and d in 14.7._
643	
644	**Answer (author).** Pandas's median wall time was 41.8% shorter than Spark's: 15.38 versus
645	26.41 s. Both halves supported this difference.
646	
647	### 15.2 (b) Phases
648	
649	> How do their phases differ?
650	
651	_Drafted with Claude Code (Opus 5.5): the phases are in 14.6 and their differences in 14.7. The
652	phases correspond by name but not by work (5)._
653	
654	**Answer (author).** Spark's model phase was shorter, but pandas saved more time in window
655	statistics, summaries and startup. This compares two implementations, not isolated engine overhead.
656	
657	### 15.3 (c) Memory and correctness
658	
659	> How do peak memory and the outputs compare?
660	
661	_Drafted with Claude Code (Opus 5.5): peak memory is in 14.6 and 14.7, and the output comparison in
662	14.8._
663	
664	**Answer (author).** Pandas's median peak total RSS was 26.6% lower than Spark's: 1.97 versus
665	2.68 GiB. All required output comparisons passed within tolerance.
666	
667	### 15.4 (d) Predictions against results
668	
669	> Where were the predictions off, and why?
670	
671	_Drafted with Claude Code (Opus 5.5) from section 11, which is unchanged, and from section 14. Time
672	items use the medians of `wall_s` and of the phases over the six measured runs, and memory items the
673	medians of peak total RSS._
674	
675	| Section 11 | Predicted | Measured | Result |
676	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
677	| S, median time | 26.5 s, band 21.2–31.8 s | 26.407 s | inside, 0.4% below the point |
678	| P, median time | 40 s, band 28–60 s | 15.377 s | outside: 61.6% below the point, 12.6 s below the band |
679	| S, median peak | 2.5–2.9 GiB | 2.680 GiB | inside |
680	| P, median peak | 0.8–1.8 GiB | 1.968 GiB | outside: 0.168 GiB above the range |
681	| Abort limits | 80 and 120 s | longest runs 27.9 and 15.7 s | no run aborted |
682	| 11.1, time | P slower than S by more than 10%, in both halves | P shorter: d = +11.030 s, with d1 and d2 of the same sign | contradicted: the ranking is reversed |
683	| 11.1, memory | P lower than S by more than 0.2 GiB, in both halves | d = +0.712 GiB, with d1 and d2 of the same sign | as predicted |
684	| 11.2, P's `model_and_path_days` | 21–44 s: the model alone 19–39 s, and building and writing the path-day rows 2–5 s | 12.134 s | below the range |
685	| 11.2, P's other phases | window statistics with input reading 1–3 s, summaries 3–6 s, checks 1–3 s, process start about 1 s | 0.308, 1.479 and 0.974 s, and 0.408 s outside the pipeline's clock | each below its estimate |
686	
687	- The model's estimate rested on an assumption (11.2): S's model phase used its eight workers at
688	  50–100% efficiency, so one core would need 3.6–7.2 ms per window for the model alone. P's whole
689	  model phase, the `path_days` write included, took 12.134 s, or 2.26 ms per window.
690	- P's model phase took 1.41 times as long as S's (12.134 against 8.622 s). The two phases do not do
691	  the same work (5), so this ratio does not measure parallel efficiency.
692	- P's peak, all in one process, exceeded the predicted range; the records do not show which data
693	  the process held at its peak.
694	
695	**Answer (author).** Spark matched its predicted ranges. Pandas was faster than predicted but used
696	more memory than predicted, reversing the expected time ranking. The estimate overstated pandas's
697	model and other phase times. The predicted memory ranking held, but the records do not explain why
698	pandas's peak exceeded its range.
699	
700	### 15.5 (e) What these measurements cannot show
701	
702	> What can these measurements not show?
703	
704	**Answer (author).** These results cover one machine and workload. No drift was detected, but that
705	does not prove constant conditions. Sampling and implementation differences limit causal claims and
706	conclusions about larger workloads.
707	
708	**Limitation added at the author's request** (drafted with Claude Code (Opus 5.5) after the Part B
709	commit). Library thread counts were not controlled or measured in either implementation. PyArrow
710	permits multithreaded reads and conversion by default; actual thread usage during the measurements
711	was not recorded. The records show that P ran in one process (14.7), not that it used a single
712	core, so "in one process on one core" in 1.1 holds only for the process count.
713

1018	## 15. Answers and limits
1019	
1020	_The questions are Claude Code's proposals of 2026-10-22. In 15.1–15.4, the parts marked as drafted
1021	give facts, computed with Claude Code (Opus 5.5) by script from batch-1's records (14) and from
1022	section 11, which is unchanged. The answers, marked "Answer (author)", are the author's, copied from
1023	the conversation of 2026-10-22._
1024	
1025	### 15.1 (a) Runtime
1026	
1027	> How did caching the members (B) and also the four tables (C) change wall time, under the rule of
1028	> section 9?
1029	
1030	_Drafted with Claude Code (Opus 5.5): the medians are in 14.6, and d1, d2 and d by pair and by phase
1031	in 14.7._
1032	
1033	**Answer (author).** B and C were slightly slower than A, but the differences were below the
1034	predefined threshold. Under the rule in section 9, there was no clear difference in runtime.
1035	
1036	### 15.2 (b) Phases and caches
1037	
1038	> Where did time move between phases, and what did the fills cost against what the cached reads
1039	> saved?
1040	
1041	_Drafted with Claude Code (Opus 5.5): the phases are in 14.6 and 14.7, and the fills, releases and
1042	reads in 14.8._
1043	
1044	**Answer (author).** B's window-statistics phase was 0.93 s longer than A's, while its model phase
1045	was 0.33 s shorter. The members fill took about 2.48 s, including data construction, so this was
1046	not all additional work. Compared with B, C's model phase increased by 1.29 s, with no net speedup
1047	in summaries or checks. Overall, the observed savings did not offset the added costs.
1048	
1049	### 15.3 (c) Memory and results
1050	
1051	> Did caching change peak memory or any result?
1052	
1053	_Drafted with Claude Code (Opus 5.5): peak memory is in 14.6 and 14.7, the caches' sizes in 14.8,
1054	and the output comparison in 14.9._
1055	
1056	**Answer (author).** Peak memory differed only slightly. All outputs passed the tolerance checks,
1057	although some floating-point summary values were not exactly equal.
1058	
1059	### 15.4 (d) Predictions against results
1060	
1061	> Where were the predictions off, and why?
1062	
1063	_Drafted with Claude Code (Opus 5.5) from section 11, which is unchanged, and from section 14. Time
1064	items use the medians of `wall_excl_capture_s` over the six measured runs, and memory items the
1065	medians of peak total RSS._

1068	| --- | --- | --- | --- |

1070	| B, median time | 26.5 s, band 21.2–31.8 s | 27.035 s | inside, 2.0% above the point |
1071	| C, median time | 27.0 s, band 21.6–35.1 s | 28.721 s | inside, 6.4% above the point |
1072	| A, B and C, median peak | 2.5–2.9, 2.5–2.9 and 2.5–3.1 GiB | 2.683, 2.678 and 2.698 GiB | inside |
1073	| Abort limits | 80, 80 and 81 s | longest runs 28.6, 29.3 and 30.5 s | no run aborted |
1074	| 11.1, sizes | members 13–15 MB; `path_days` about 0.19 GiB; the small tables under 3 MB each; nothing on disk | 13.77 MB; 0.188 GiB (202.21 MB); 0.48, 1.03 and 0.91 MB; 0 bytes on disk | as predicted |
1075	| 11.1, fill and release times | members 0.3–1.2 s; `path_days` 0.3–1.5 s; the small tables under 0.3 s each; releases under 0.1 s | members 2.481 s (B) and 2.467 s (C); `path_days` 1.325 s; 0.075–0.137 s; releases at most 0.005 s | members above the range; the others as predicted |
1076	| 11.1, files | 1, 40, 8 and 1 | 1, 40, 8 and 1 in all 24 runs | as predicted |

1085	**Answer (author).** I underestimated the members fill time, and the prediction of exact equality
1086	did not hold. A different order of floating-point addition is a plausible explanation, but the
1087	specific mechanism has not been established. C's additional caching also produced less net benefit
1088	than expected, and its checks were not consistently faster than B's.
1089	
1090	### 15.5 (e) What these measurements cannot show
1091	
1092	> What can these measurements not show?
1093	
1094	**Answer (author).** These results apply to this machine, workload and caching strategy. CPU time
1095	and garbage collection were not measured, so the conclusions cannot be generalized to all Spark
1096	workloads.

93	        except psutil.NoSuchProcess:
94	            return

97	                procs = [root, *root.children(recursive=True)]
98	            except psutil.NoSuchProcess:
99	                break
100	            total, by_kind, counted = 0, {}, 0

104	                except (psutil.NoSuchProcess, psutil.AccessDenied, psutil.ZombieProcess):

106	                total += rss
107	                by_kind[kind] = by_kind.get(kind, 0) + rss

114	            if total > self.threshold and self.first_exceeded_at is None:

120	        self.join()

127	def run_status(exit_code: int, exceeded: bool) -> tuple[str, list[str]]:
128	    """Primary status and every reason to stop. Pipeline exit codes: 0 ok, 1 checks failed, other = failed."""
129	    reasons = []
130	    if exit_code not in (0, 1):
131	        reasons.append(f"failed (exit code {exit_code})")
132	    if exit_code == 1:
133	        reasons.append("checks_failed")
134	    if exceeded:
135	        reasons.append("memory_threshold_exceeded")
136	    if exit_code not in (0, 1):
137	        return "failed", reasons
138	    if exit_code == 1:
139	        return "checks_failed", reasons
140	    return ("memory_threshold_exceeded" if exceeded else "ok"), reasons
141	
142	
143	def run_protocol(make_command: Callable[[str], Sequence[str]], run_dir_of: Callable[[str], Path], log_dir: Path,
144	                 repeats: int, interval: float = DEFAULT_INTERVAL,
145	                 threshold_fraction: float = DEFAULT_THRESHOLD_FRACTION) -> dict:
146	    total_ram = psutil.virtual_memory().total
147	    threshold = threshold_fraction * total_ram
148	    stamp = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ")
149	    log_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
150	    runs, stop_reason = [], None
151	    for i in range(repeats):
152	        run_id = f"run-{stamp}-{i + 1}"
153	        free_before = psutil.virtual_memory().available
154	        started_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
155	        log_path = log_dir / f"{run_id}.log"
156	        t0 = time.perf_counter()
157	        with log_path.open("w") as log:
158	            proc = subprocess.Popen(list(make_command(run_id)), stdout=log, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
159	            sampler = TreeSampler(proc.pid, interval, threshold)
160	            sampler.start()
161	            exit_code = proc.wait()
162	            sampler.stop()
163	        wall = time.perf_counter() - t0
164	        status, reasons = run_status(exit_code, sampler.exceeded)
165	        measurement = {
166	            "warmup": i == 0, "exit_code": exit_code, "protocol_status": status, "stop_reasons": reasons,
167	            "wall_seconds": round(wall, 3), "started_at_utc": started_at, "log": str(log_path),
168	            "free_memory_before_bytes": free_before, "peak_rss_total_bytes": sampler.peak_total,
169	            "peak_rss_by_kind_bytes": sampler.peak_by_kind, "samples": sampler.samples,
170	            "sample_interval_seconds": interval, "max_processes_seen": sampler.max_processes,
171	            "threshold_bytes": int(threshold), "threshold_first_exceeded_after_seconds": sampler.first_exceeded_at,
172	            "limits": LIMITS,
173	        }
174	        run_json = run_dir_of(run_id) / "run.json"

Every command was run on the project's machine\nthat day with the results described here; the figures and the pipeline run went to a scratch folder\ninstead of `data/figures-demo` and `data/outputs-demo`._\n\n**Before you start.** Python 3.12, Java 17 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/); run everything from\nthe repository root. The data is not in Git. Steps 2 and 3 need the snapshot `full-2026-10-12`, its\nwindow definitions, the run of record and the experiments' measurement CSVs under `data/`, which\nexist only on the machine that produced them. On a fresh clone, run the README's\n[Running](../README.md#running) section first; it makes a new snapshot and run, on which steps 1, 3\nand 4 work with the new paths.\n\n## 1. Tests\n\n```bash\nuv sync\nuv run --group measure --group plots pytest\n```\n\nEvery test passes, without network, in about five minutes. One test can fail intermittently (see\n[the note at the end](#a-known-intermittent-test-failure)).\n\n## 2. The figures and their check\n\n```bash\nuv run --group plots python -m etf_risk.plots --check\nuv run --group plots python -m etf_risk.plots --out data/figures-demo\ndiff -rq docs/figures data/figures-demo && echo identical\n```\n\nThe first command prints each figure's checked numbers and ends with `documented values: all\nmatch`: every number it compares with spec §8, data-sources.md and the experiment documents is the\nsame. The second redraws the twelve figures and `figures.json`, and `diff` compares them with the\ncommitted ones: in the same environment they are byte-identical. [results.md](results.md) shows the\nfigures with the findings and limitations.\n\n## 3. The SQL analyses of the run of record\n\n```bash\nRUN=data/outputs/windows/full-2026-10-12/rolling-252-s21-r2/run-20261013T043848Z-2\nuv run python analysis/sql_overview.py $RUN\nuv run python analysis/sql_comparison.py $RUN\nuv run python analysis/sql_sensitivity.py $RUN\n```\n\nAbout 10 s each. Their last tables hold the numbers of spec §8 and of the table in results.md,\nsection 2: for example 529, 466, 311, 174 and 310 windows, the 2x return above twice the 1x return\nin 219 of AAPL's 517 compared windows, and TSLA's median 2x return of −12.3% (`-0.1225…`) without\nthe windows that use an unverified day. `sql_overview.py` also prints the `paired` schema, a few rows\nand the physical plan of its query.\n\n## 4. A small pipeline run and its independent check\n\n```bash\nuv run python -m etf_risk.spark_pipeline --windows data/windows/full-2026-10-12/calendar-year-r2 --out-root data/outputs-demo --run-id demo-1\nuv run python -m etf_risk.verify --run data/outputs-demo/full-2026-10-12/calendar-year-r2/demo-1\n```\n\nThe first runs the model in Spark over the 151 calendar-year windows, a labeled supplement to the\nrolling windows, with every check at full scale; it prints `demo-1: ok` with the row counts and the\nrun folder, then `ok` for each group of checks. The second compares a sample of windows with an\nindependent Python computation and reports 0 mismatches. The outputs go to `data/outputs-demo/`,\noutside Git; nothing is overwritten, so another run needs a new `--run-id`.\n\n## A known intermittent test failure\n\n`test_measure_runs_the_pandas_pipeline_in_fresh_processes` in `tests/test_pandas_pipeline.py` can\nfail with `AssertionError: assert {'driver', 'spark_jvm'} == {'driver'}`, or with `'other'` in\nplace of `'spark_jvm'`. The test times the pandas pipeline with `etf_risk.measure` and expects to\nsee only the pipeline's own process. About 0.4–0.6 s after it starts, though, the pipeline runs\nshort helper commands for its run record (`git` twice, `uname` and `file` through\n`platform.platform()`, and `java -version`). When one of measure's samples, taken every 0.25 s,\nfalls while a helper is running, measure records it: `java` as `spark_jvm`, the others as `other`.\n\n- **Reproduced:** the test failed this way in 1 of 20 runs, and measure's sampler recorded a helper\n  in 2 of 15 pipeline runs on an idle machine and in 4 of 15 under CPU load.\n- **Not established:** the failure first seen, in a full test run, kept no traceback, so that it had\n  the same cause is likely but not shown.\n- **Not affected:** the pipeline's outputs, and the pandas baseline's records, in which all eight P\n  runs recorded only the pipeline's process.\n- **Not fixed:** the test's assertion could tolerate the helpers, or measure could count a `java`\n  process as `spark_jvm` only when it runs Spark; neither change has been made.\n"
}

51	![M2: the 2x log gap against minus the realized variance](figures/m2-log-gap-vs-variance.png)

53	Under the model, the gap to twice the underlying has an exact form. Each day
54	`(1 + r)² − (1 + 2r) = r²`, so in log terms a 2x window without a breach always falls short of twice
55	the underlying, by about the window's realized variance: `log(1 + R_2x) − 2 log(1 + R_1x) = Σ log(1 − (r/(1 + r))²) ≈ −Σ r²`. In
56	simple returns, compounding can still lift the 2x return above twice the underlying's in strong,
57	steady trends (spec §8, expectation 1). The exact identity held in all 1,778 windows without a
58	breach, and the approximation `−Σ r²` was close: the median relative error per ticker lay between
59	−1.2% (NVDA) and +0.3% (TSLA) (M2).
60	
61	![M3: 2x against 1x maximum drawdown, with the bound](figures/m3-drawdown-bound.png)
62	
63	For drawdowns, the model implies `MDD_2x ≥ 1 − (1 − MDD_1x)²` for every window without a breach: a
64	30% drawdown at 1x means at least 51% at 2x (spec §8, expectation 2). No window fell below this
65	bound (M3).

1	# Leveraged ETF Risk Analytics — results
2	
3	Author: I decided which figures to make and how the work was divided: Claude Code wrote the figure
4	code and drafted the facts below, and the conclusions (section 7) are mine.
5	
6	_Drafted with Claude Code (Opus 5.5) on 2026-10-22 from the figures' checked numbers
7	([figures/figures.json](figures/figures.json)), [spec.md](spec.md) §8,
8	[data-sources.md](data-sources.md) and the four experiment documents, which hold the design, records
9	and details behind every number here._
10	
11	This is the project's final write-up: what the results show, with the twelve figures, and what they
12	cannot show. The results describe historical 252-trading-day windows of five tickers, replayed by a
13	daily-reset 1x/2x model that ignores fees, financing and execution; they are not forecasts. The
14	figures are drawn from the result files by `etf_risk.plots` and never edited by hand; its `--check`
15	compares their numbers with the values the documents report (section 8, [demo.md](demo.md)).
16	
17	## 1. Data and windows
18	
19	![D1: daily returns of the snapshot, with the unverified extreme days](figures/d1-daily-returns.png)
20	
21	Daily returns of NVDA, AAPL, MSFT, TSLA and QQQ come from Yahoo Finance (snapshot
22	`full-2026-10-12`), each from its first trading day to 2025-12-31 (D1). The data is partially
23	checked, not fully verified ([data-sources.md](data-sources.md)): trading dates match the NYSE
24	schedule and Adj Close is consistent with Yahoo's own dividend records, but no second source has
25	been compared, and 36 extreme days are **unverified** (NVDA 18, TSLA 9, AAPL 8, MSFT 1, QQQ 0). They
26	stay in the data and are flagged.
27	
28	![D2: entry dates of the rolling windows, by ticker](figures/d2-window-entry-dates.png)
29	
30	The run of record (`rolling-252-s21-r2`, protocol `20261013T043848Z`) holds 1,790 windows of 252
31	trading days, a new one every 21 trading days on a start grid shared by all tickers (D2). 239 of
32	them (13%) use an unverified day, among them 30% of NVDA's and 33% of TSLA's. Consecutive windows
33	share most of their days, so the windows describe one history per ticker, not independent samples.
34	Every check of the run passed: 46 check tests with no violation on all 1,790 windows, and an
35	independent Python computation matched all 1,074 paths it compared (spec §8).
36	
37	## 2. Path dependence (question 1)
38	
39	![M1: the 2x window return against twice the 1x return](figures/m1-returns-2x-vs-1x.png)
40	
41	| | AAPL | MSFT | NVDA | TSLA | QQQ |
42	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
43	| Windows | 529 | 466 | 311 | 174 | 310 |
44	| Median 1x return | 24.4% | 22.8% | 39.5% | 22.5% | 16.6% |
45	| Median 2x return | 35.2% (517 windows) | 39.9% | 51.3% | 13.5% | 31.4% |
46	| 2x return above twice the 1x return | 219 of 517 (42.4%) | 164 of 466 (35.2%) | 141 of 311 (45.3%) | 43 of 174 (24.7%) | 140 of 310 (45.2%) |
47	
48	For every ticker, the daily-reset 2x return exceeded twice the 1x return in fewer than half of the
49	windows (M1). QQQ holds the other four, so it is shown on its own, never pooled with them.
50	
51	![M2: the 2x log gap against minus the realized variance](figures/m2-log-gap-vs-variance.png)
52	
53	Under the model, the gap to twice the underlying has an exact form. Each day
54	`(1 + r)² − (1 + 2r) = r²`, so in log terms a 2x window without a breach always falls short of
55	twice the underlying, by about the window's realized variance:
56	
57	```text
58	log(1 + R_2x) − 2 log(1 + R_1x) = Σ log(1 − (r_t / (1 + r_t))²) ≈ −Σ r_t²
59	```
60	
61	In simple returns, compounding can still lift the 2x return above twice the underlying's in strong,
62	steady trends (spec §8, expectation 1). The exact identity held in all 1,778 windows without a
63	breach. The approximation `−Σ r²` was close: its median relative error per ticker lay between
64	−1.2% (NVDA) and +0.3% (TSLA) (M2).
65	
66	![M3: 2x against 1x maximum drawdown, with the bound](figures/m3-drawdown-bound.png)
67	
68	For drawdowns, the model implies `MDD_2x ≥ 1 − (1 − MDD_1x)²` for every window without a
69	breach: a 30% drawdown at 1x means at least 51% at 2x (spec §8, expectation 2). No window fell
70	below this bound (M3).
71	
72	![M5: the 2x NAV of the windows whose 2x path was breached](figures/m5-breached-windows.png)
73	
74	At 2x, only a daily loss of 50% or more ends a path (`1 + 2r ≤ 0`), and the snapshot has one such
75	day: AAPL on 2000-09-29 (−51.9%), which is unverified. The 12 AAPL windows that contain it have no
76	2x return; they are left out of the 2x statistics and reported apart, with their values before the
77	breach (M5). A breach is a model boundary, not a modeled liquidation of a real fund.
78	
79	## 3. Rebalancing (question 2)
80	
81	![M4: 2x mean daily turnover per window, by ticker](figures/m4-turnover-2x.png)
82	
83	To return to 2x exposure at each close, the model trades `L(L − 1) r = 2r` of the day's starting
84	NAV, adding exposure after up days and cutting it after down days, so the daily turnover is `2|r|`
85	(spec §3; §8, expectation 4). The median of the 2x mean daily turnover per window ranged from 1.8%
86	of NAV (QQQ) to 5.0% (TSLA) (M4). These are magnitudes the model implies, not observed trading or
87	market impact.
88	
89	## 4. Sensitivity to the unverified days
90	
91	![S1: median window returns with and without the windows that use an unverified day](figures/s1-sensitivity-medians.png)
92	
93	Leaving out the 239 windows that use an unverified day moves some medians noticeably: TSLA's median
94	2x return falls from 13.5% (174 windows) to −12.3% (117), while AAPL's rises from 35.2% (517) to
95	48.5% (451); QQQ has no such window (S1). The flagged windows are a non-random subset, periods with
96	extreme market days, so this shows how much the results depend on those periods, not whether those
97	days are data errors.
98	
99	## 5. Spark performance (question 3)
100	
101	Runtime and memory were measured on one Apple Silicon laptop (8 cores, 8 GiB RAM), with Spark in
102	local mode, a fresh process per run, and memory as the summed resident memory of the run's
103	processes, sampled every 0.25 s. Each experiment's design and predictions were committed before any
104	measured run, and each figure keeps that experiment's own time metric: `wall_s`, or
105	`wall_excl_capture_s` (the wall time without recording the execution plans) where plans were
106	recorded.
107	
108	![X1: stride experiment, runtime and peak memory against the number of windows](figures/x1-stride-experiment.png)
109	
110	**Workload size** ([experiments.md](experiments.md)). Going from stride 21 to stride 7 (1,790 to
111	5,364 windows) raised the median `wall_s` from 22.2 to 25.7 s (20.3 s at stride 14) and the median
112	peak from 2.62 to 2.70 GiB. A linear fit over the three strides gives an intercept of 18.8 s (85% of
113	the stride-21 median) and 1.2 ms per window: an estimate from three points, not measured overhead.
114	A repeated stride-21 protocol had an 18.3% shorter median than the first, beyond the 10% drift
115	tolerance, so the comparisons across strides are marked as affected; stride 3 (40.2 s, 2.73 GiB) is
116	exploratory only. At stride 21 these runs took half the run of record's time (44.7 s) and about
117	twice its memory (1.27 GiB); the records do not establish why.
118	
119	![X2: shuffle-partition experiment](figures/x2-shuffle-partition-experiment.png)
120	
121	**Shuffle partitions** ([partition-experiment.md](partition-experiment.md), stride 7). The median
122	`wall_excl_capture_s` was 26.5 s with Spark's defaults (A: 200 shuffle partitions, AQE coalescing
123	on), 44.6 s with coalescing off (B) and 25.3 s with 8 partitions and coalescing off (C). B's median
124	was 69% longer than A's and 77% longer than C's, in both halves of the order; A and C showed no
125	clear difference. In B every shuffle read used all 200 partitions, its summed stage task counts were
126	3.3 to 19.7 times A's, it wrote 1,584 output files against A's 50, and one join stayed a sort-merge
127	join where AQE chose a broadcast join in A and C; the records cannot separate these costs. Median
128	peaks were 2.69 GiB in all three.
129	
130	![X3: pandas baseline](figures/x3-pandas-baseline.png)
131	
132	**Spark against pandas** ([pandas-baseline.md](pandas-baseline.md), stride 7). A pandas
133	implementation of the same computation, running in one process, had a 41.8% shorter median `wall_s`
134	than the Spark pipeline at Spark's defaults (15.4 against 26.4 s) and a 26.6% lower median peak
135	(1.97 against 2.68 GiB), in both halves of the order; the prediction had put it at about 40 s. Its
136	model phase took longer (12.1 against 8.6 s), its other phases less time, and it starts no Spark
137	session. Both call the same model function but read, aggregate and write in their own ways, so this
138	is an end-to-end comparison of two implementations, not a measure of Spark's overhead. PyArrow
139	permits multithreaded reads and conversion by default; actual thread usage during the measurements
140	was not recorded.
141	
142	![X4: caching experiment](figures/x4-caching-experiment.png)
143	
144	**Caching** ([caching-experiment.md](caching-experiment.md), stride 7). With the window-member rows
145	cached (B), or those and the four tables read back after each phase (C), the median
146	`wall_excl_capture_s` was 27.0 and 28.7 s against 26.5 s without a cache (A): B and C were 2.1% and
147	8.4% slower than A, slower in each half but below the 10% threshold, so there was no clear
148	difference. Caching the members lengthened the window statistics by 0.93 s and shortened the model
149	phase by 0.33 s; C's further caches lengthened the model phase by 1.29 s, with no observed net
150	saving in the summaries or checks. Median peaks were 2.68–2.70 GiB.
151	
152	## 6. Limitations
153	
154	- **Data.** One source, partially checked. Until a second source is compared, the 36 unverified
155	  extreme days may be data errors as well as market events. A same-day re-download differed by up
156	  to 1.9e−6 in daily returns, and the data's terms of use have not been reviewed
157	  ([data-sources.md](data-sources.md)).
158	- **Windows.** Overlapping windows of five tickers describe one history each, not independent
159	  samples, so no probability statements are made. QQQ holds the other four, all five share
160	  market-wide shocks, and the four stocks are survivors.
161	- **Model.** No fees, financing, interest on cash, tracking error or trading costs, and one reset
162	  at each close, so no NAV here forecasts a real fund; a breach is a model boundary (spec §3).
163	- **Performance.** One machine, one dataset and Spark's local mode, with three measured runs per
164	  protocol and six per configuration. RSS sampled every 0.25 s can miss shorter peaks, and summed
165	  RSS counts shared pages once per process. CPU time, garbage collection and spilling were not
166	  measured, so the records cannot separate the mechanisms behind the differences. Conditions
167	  varied: drift in the stride experiment, machine checks only before the first protocol and a
168	  two-hour break in the shuffle-partition experiment, and uneven gaps in the caching experiment.
169	- **Figures.** Regenerating them gives byte-identical files only in the same environment: the
170	  lockfile's packages, matplotlib's bundled fonts and the same platform.
171	
172	## 7. Conclusions (author)

1	# Demo
2	
3	A short walk-through on the machine that holds the project's data: the tests, the figures and their

5	About ten minutes, most of it the test suite.
6	
7	_Drafted with Claude Code (Opus 5.5) on 2026-10-22 and 2026-10-23. Every command was run on the
8	project's machine on those days with the results described here; the figures and the pipeline run
9	went to a scratch folder instead of `data/figures-demo` and `data/outputs-demo`._
10	
11	**Before you start.** Python 3.12, Java 17 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/); run everything from
12	the repository root. Step 1 needs no data. The data is not in Git: steps 2 to 4 need the snapshot
13	`full-2026-10-12` with its window definitions, the run of record and, for step 2, the experiments'
14	measurement CSVs under `data/`, which exist only on the machine that produced them. On a fresh
15	clone, follow the README's [Running](../README.md#running) section first: it builds a new snapshot
16	and run, and steps 3 and 4 then work with those paths (step 4 with the calendar-year windows of the

19	## 1. Tests
20	
21	```bash
22	uv sync
23	uv run --group measure --group plots pytest

33	uv run --group plots python -m etf_risk.plots --out data/figures-demo
34	diff -rq docs/figures data/figures-demo && echo identical
35	```
36	
37	The first command prints each figure's checked numbers and ends with `documented values: all
38	match`: every number it compares with spec §8, data-sources.md and the experiment documents is the
39	same. The second redraws the twelve figures and `figures.json`, and `diff` compares them with the
40	committed ones: in the same environment they are byte-identical. [results.md](results.md) shows the
41	figures with the findings and limitations.

48	uv run python analysis/sql_comparison.py $RUN

54	in 219 of AAPL's 517 compared windows, and TSLA's median 2x return of −12.3% (`-0.1225…`)
55	without the windows that use an unverified day. `sql_overview.py` also prints the `paired`

59	
60	```bash
61	uv run python -m etf_risk.spark_pipeline --windows data/windows/full-2026-10-12/calendar-year-r2 --out-root data/outputs-demo --run-id demo-1
62	uv run python -m etf_risk.verify --run data/outputs-demo/full-2026-10-12/calendar-year-r2/demo-1
63	```

65	The first runs the model in Spark over the 151 calendar-year windows, a labeled supplement to the
66	rolling windows, with every check at full scale, in about 20 s: it prints `demo-1: ok` with the row
67	counts (151 windows, 75,971 path-day rows) and the run folder, then `ok` for each of the ten groups
68	of checks. The second compares a sample of windows with an independent Python computation (53
69	windows and 106 paths on 2026-10-23) and reports 0 mismatches; both find the one breached window,
70	AAPL's calendar year 2000. The outputs go to `data/outputs-demo/`, outside Git; nothing is
71	overwritten, so another run needs a new `--run-id`.

73	## A known intermittent test failure
74	
75	`test_measure_runs_the_pandas_pipeline_in_fresh_processes` in `tests/test_pandas_pipeline.py` can
76	fail with `AssertionError: assert {'driver', 'spark_jvm'} == {'driver'}`, or with `'other'` in
77	place of `'spark_jvm'`. The test times the pandas pipeline with `etf_risk.measure` and expects to
78	see only the pipeline's own process. About 0.4–0.6 s after it starts, though, the pipeline runs
79	short helper commands for its run record (`git` twice, `uname` and `file` through
80	`platform.platform()`, and `java -version`). When one of measure's samples, taken every 0.25 s,
81	falls while a helper is running, measure records it: `java` as `spark_jvm`, the others as `other`.

## The intermittent test failure

- **What failed:** the original run kept only the test name and the summary line. My output filter dropped the traceback, and pytest's temporary folders for that run were since deleted.
- **Likely cause:** before it computes anything, the pandas pipeline starts short helper commands for its run record: `git` twice, `uname` and `file`, and `java -version` ([pandas_pipeline.py:577](src/etf_risk/pandas_pipeline.py#L577)).
  - These run about 0.4–0.6 s after start, around the memory sampler's third sample.
  - The sampler labels any `java` process `spark_jvm` ([measure.py:64-73](src/etf_risk/measure.py#L64-L73)) and the others `other`.
  - The test expects only the pipeline's own process ([test_pandas_pipeline.py:240](tests/test_pandas_pipeline.py#L240)), so a sample that catches a helper fails it.
- **Reproduced:**
  - The real test failed in 1 of 20 runs with `AssertionError: assert {'driver', 'spark_jvm'} == {'driver'}`. The full output is in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-[REDACTED:user]-leveraged-etf-risk-analytics/c82fe879-2a08-4e8f-a4c7-740b70b55e9a/scratchpad/test-repeats/run-1.txt
  - The sampler itself caught a helper in 2 of 15 pipeline runs on an idle machine and 4 of 15 under CPU load.
- **Still uncertain:** the original failure's error message was never recorded, so it most likely had the same cause, but that isn't established. These rates come from small samples; an earlier probe of mine saw 0 in 12.
- **What's affected:** neither the pipeline's outputs nor the pandas baseline's records. All 8 pandas runs recorded only the pipeline's own process.
- **Fix, not made (it's outside Stage 4):** two options.
  - Relax the test. That's simplest, but the test would then also accept a real Spark JVM.
  - Make the sampler label `java` as `spark_jvm` only when it is actually running Spark, and let the test accept `other`. That keeps what the test is meant to check, but changes how future measurements label processes.

  I lean to the second, with a note in the experiment documents.
